contexts.context: Mean test macro F1 is \m{BAFone} for static CCD, \m{BBFone} for sequential CCD and \m{BCFone} for MO-TPE. The observed differences do not establish a method ranking. Global response prediction depends on both sampling coverage and surrogate choice, so it is evaluated separately from optimizer performance. The original \m{BCap}\,$\mu$s calibration-derived threshold is unmet; capacity-matched and reference-point sensitivity analyses are reported explicitly as post hoc. The study demonstrates a reproducible comparison of selection, response modeling and diagnostic explanations. It does not establish general efficiency gains or the effectiveness of SHAP-driven acquisition.

contexts.section: A planned design with stochastic nuisance blocks
contexts.context: The historical design contains \m{ADesign} fitted evaluations across \m{ABlocks} data-split blocks. It studies learning rate, maximum depth, row subsampling and leaf-weight regularization. A globally randomized, preplanned face-centered CCD supplies the observations. The factorial and augmented analyses are hierarchical analyses of that completed design; they are not evidence that an early result adaptively determined whether the later points were run.

contexts.section: A planned design with stochastic nuisance blocks
contexts.context: California Housing~\cite{housing} is divided into \m{ASplittrain}\% training, \m{ASplitval}\% validation and \m{ASplittest}\% test data, with \m{ACapacity} boosting trees per model. The model predicts median house values; RMSE retains the dataset's target scale. The split is randomized, so this study does not test transfer to geographically separated regions. Early exploratory work exposed test outcomes; later access restrictions cannot undo that exposure.

The recorded RMSE limits are \m{DesirabilityErrorLow} and \m{DesirabilityErrorHigh}; latency limits are \m{DesirabilityLatencyLow} and \m{DesirabilityLatencyHigh}\,$\mu$s. The shape exponents and response weights equal \m{DesirabilityExponent}. These are preference settings, not estimated physical constants. Selected candidates receive separate confirmation evaluations.

contexts.section: Useful structure, but not a perfect surface
contexts.context: The factorial-to-center curvature statistic is \m{ACurvature}. The response clearly departs from a flat plane over the tested range. The block-variance analysis reports an RMSE intraclass correlation of \m{AIcc}\%. This supports treating data partition as a meaningful nuisance condition rather than ignoring it.

contexts.section: Useful structure, but not a perfect surface
contexts.context: However, strong global structure is not the same as local predictive accuracy. The RMSE surface has a lack-of-fit statistic of \m{ALof}. A smooth quadratic equation captures major trends yet misses some systematic response behavior. The curvature contrast uses center-point pure error, whereas the stored lack-of-fit analysis has a different replicate-error decomposition. These denominators must not be conflated, and neither automatically represents uncertainty over all future datasets.

contexts.section: Useful structure, but not a perfect surface
contexts.context: The lowest learning rate, \m{ALowRate}, occurs in \m{ALowCount} of \m{ADesign} runs (\m{ALowPct}\%); that allocation follows the CCD geometry. The issue is whether the chosen range learns adequately under the fixed tree budget. New post-hoc diagnostics give lack-of-fit $F=\m{PostLogLof}$ after log-transforming RMSE and $F=\m{PostRestrictedLof}$ after excluding that low-rate face. The restricted fit has $R^2=\m{PostRestrictedRtwo}$ but rank \m{PostRestrictedRank} of \m{PostRestrictedColumns}: its remaining learning-rate linear and squared terms are aliased. Thus neither transformation nor exclusion establishes an adequate quadratic model or localizes all misspecification to the low-rate face.

Table~\ref{tab:aconfirm} compares the surface with confirmation on new data-split seeds, disjoint from the design's split seeds but using the same housing dataset. The compromise candidate's observed validation RMSE falls within its interval. The accuracy-focused candidate lies above its upper bound; its observed-minus-predicted gap is \m{AAccuracyBias} RMSE. These are working-model intervals from a demonstrably imperfect surface; the gap combines model inadequacy and split variation rather than identifying either cause alone.

\caption{Phase A validation-RMSE confirmation. Model-based \m{AIntervalLevel}\% prediction intervals target the mean of \m{AConfirmationCount} confirmation runs per candidate; the observed column is that mean. The intervals do not cover every possible future dataset outcome.}\label{tab:aconfirm}\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:abench} summarizes \m{ARepeats} searches per method, with \m{AEvaluationCount} retraining evaluations per selection. Its error SD describes variability between search-level mean test errors. The displayed zero for DOE accuracy reflects repeated selection of the same configuration and the same evaluation seeds; it does not mean error-free prediction or zero retraining variability.

Latency also exposes a measurement problem. At the predeclared \m{ACap}\,$\mu$s threshold, Constrained TPE appears feasible in \m{ASearchFeasible} of \m{ARepeats} searches but only \m{AVerifiedFeasible} selections remain feasible under benchmark verification. The short online timing and longer final measurement differ in cost and precision. Selection near a noisy boundary can amplify their disagreement. The data do not establish one unique causal explanation for the discrepancy.

The IMDb movie-review dataset~\cite{imdb} supplies \m{BDev} development documents and \m{BTest} test documents after HTML removal, whitespace normalization and exact-text deduplication. Official test copies are retained when duplicates span the two partitions. Term frequency--inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) converts each document into a sparse vector of word and word-pair weights, using at most \m{BVocab} features and sublinear term frequency. Vocabulary and weights are fitted within each training fold, so validation text does not determine that fold's representation.

The development pool is partitioned into \m{BBlocks} stratified folds. Every method evaluates a proposed configuration on the same folds and receives the mean response across them. The folds are useful shared nuisance conditions, but their training observations overlap. Different optimizer seeds on those folds do not create independently sampled datasets.

The lower learning-rate boundary is now \m{BRateLow}. Development calibration compares tree budgets before fixing the main study's capacity. At the low rate, observed calibration macro F1 changes from \m{CalSmall} at \m{CalSmallTrees} trees to \m{CalLarge} at \m{BTrees} trees. The capacity rule chooses the smallest tested budget whose low-rate F1 is within \m{BCalTolerance} of the largest tested budget, selecting \m{BTrees} trees. This reduces the low-capacity problem within the tested grid; it does not prove that larger models cannot improve.

Models are trained on an \AcceleratorName{} accelerator. Prediction latency and local word-response probabilities are measured on CPU. This separates training acceleration from the inference operation being evaluated.

A proposed coordinate is evaluated on every development fold, so model-fit count must not be confused with unique configuration count.

contexts.section: The timing protocol and what the threshold means
contexts.context: The common measurement operation uses \m{BWarmups} warmups followed by \m{BCalls} timed predictions per interface, with CPU affinity and single-thread prediction recorded. The primary operation includes fresh DMatrix construction plus prediction of one already-vectorized document; \texttt{inplace\_predict} is recorded separately. Raw-text TF-IDF transformation is excluded.

contexts.section: The timing protocol and what the threshold means
contexts.context: The original threshold, \m{BCap}\,$\mu$s, pools calibration timings from different tree budgets. It is low relative to the main study's selected capacity, making failure plausible in advance, but calibration does not prove universal infeasibility. A post-hoc capacity-matched reference is \m{PostCapacity}\,$\mu$s, the median of all calibration timings at the selected tree budget. Both references are descriptive, not deployment requirements. Hypervolume uses loss reference \m{BReferenceLoss} and latency reference \m{BReference}\,$\mu$s; the latency reference is twice the largest calibration median.

contexts.section: Local word explanations answer a separate question
contexts.context: The word study asks how the probability from one fixed sentiment classifier changes when selected word-feature weights are attenuated. This classifier uses the first sequential-CCD selection, refitted on the training portion of the first development fold; explanations concern that fold's validation documents. A local CCD varies the strongest present unigram features, fits a quadratic probability surface and evaluates fidelity on \m{BWordConfirm} unused perturbations per document. Exact pairwise Shapley values describe the declared feature-weight game.

contexts.section: Local word explanations answer a separate question
contexts.context: The study covers \m{BWordDocs} eligible development-validation documents chosen by a fixed label-independent rule. The largest document-level confirmation RMSE is \m{BWordMaxError} probability units. Fidelity varies: some local response functions are simple under these perturbations, while others are less well represented by a quadratic surface.

contexts.section: Local word explanations answer a separate question
contexts.context: The original perturbations attenuate selected unigram weights while fixing other features, including bigrams, without renormalization. They describe a conditional feature-weight game rather than rewritten sentences. The illustrated example's maximum recorded endpoint-game pair interaction is \m{PostWordInteractionMax}; zero endpoint interactions do not imply a quadratic continuous probability response. LIME~\cite{lime} and classifier TreeSHAP address related local-explanation questions but were not matched experimental arms, so this study does not establish superiority over either.

\item \textbf{Replication and information allocation.} Phase B has \m{BRepeats} search repeats and only \m{PostAdaptiveCoordinates} infill coordinates per sequential search. It cannot establish modest method advantages or general conclusions about adaptive design. Phase A compares replicated planned coordinates with broader fixed-split searches. The frozen-model document bootstrap does not resolve either asymmetry. No matched random-search, default-XGBoost or linear-text-classifier arm was included in Phase B.

\item \textbf{Design geometry and explanation.} Face-centered CCD concentrates observations at corners, axial points and repeated centers. Space-filling computer-experiment designs~\cite{sacks,santner} offer a relevant alternative for GP modeling. Global confirmation favors coverage; it is not the same target as finding a good local operating point. Shared-data explanation agreement is not ground truth. The local word study covers \m{BWordDocs} selected documents and a small conditional perturbation game.

contexts.section: Run Phase B with CUDA training or CPU training
contexts.context: CUDA training requires a CUDA-enabled XGBoost installation and compatible NVIDIA hardware and driver. The measured run records an \AcceleratorName{}; other compatible hardware can run the method but may produce different timings. CUDA accelerates classifier training; surrogate analysis and the prediction-latency operation remain on CPU.
